2. Pull in BIRDBASE1:

This dataset provides a thorough, literature based review of all bird species and includes habitat and foraging information that can be used to assign birds to guilds.

The primary habitat and primary diet values were used but it’s worth noting that BIRDBASE provides information on how each bird species fits into each type. This could help if a more involved analysis is requested.

  1. Merge ebird with BIRDBASE to get guild information:

The two datasets can easily be merged by the scientific name. The final dataset was heavily truncated to include on the data that is needed for this analysis.

Habitat

Grouping the Klamath bird species by the primary habitat type. Habitat types include: Grassland, Sea, Wetland, Coastal, Riparian, Artificial, Shrub, Rocky, Plains, Woodland, Forest, Savanna, Desert. The number of species across months and years are grouped by each habitat type to create the habitat dataset.

Foraging

Grouping the Klamath bird species by the primary diet type. Diet types include: Plant, Carnivore, Vertebrate, Fish, Invertebrate, Omnivore, Seed, Herbivore, Scavenger, Nectar, Fruit. The number of species across months and years are grouped by each diet type to create the foraging dataset.

Build Guild based on diet and habitat

Bird species were grouped into functional guilds based on a combination of primary diet and primary habitat. Diet × habitat guilds were defined for each observation by pairing the species’ primary diet category with its primary habitat category. Species richness was summarized by guild across months and years, and guilds were ranked by total species richness.

There are 69 guilds. The top 10 are:

  1. Şekercioğlu, Çağan H; Kittelberger, Kyle D.; Mota, Flávia; Buxton, Amy N.; Orton, Nikolas; DeNiro, Adara; et al. (2025). BIRDBASE: A Global Database of Avian Biogeography, Conservation, Ecology and Life History Traits. figshare. Dataset. https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.27051040.v1↩︎

  2. Donnelly, J. P., Moore, J. N., Casazza, M. L., & Coons, S. P. (2022). Functional wetland loss drives emerging risks to waterbird migration networks. Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution, 10, 844278. https://doi.org/10.3389/fevo.2022.844278↩︎
